title: Growing the Efficient Frontier on Panel Trees

p.t: Estimating the mean-variance efficient (MVE) frontier remains crucial in asset pricing and investment management. However, attempting to reach the efficient frontier by estimating the tangency portfolio from the high-dimensional, unbalanced panel of individual asset returns proves impracticable (Cochrane, 2009). Empirical asset pricing studies address the challenge by considering a "diversified" set of assets as basis portfolios and identifying a few common factors to achieve multi-factor portfolio efficiency (Fama, 1996). These approaches for using left-hand-side test assets and right-hand-side risk factors are statistically equivalent in terms of spanning the efficient frontier (Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken, 1989), because under the MVE framework with zero alphas, the collective Sharpe ratios of test assets equal those of risk factors. However, popular factor models hardly span the common test asset universe (e.g., Kozak et al., 2018;Daniel et al., 2020;Lopez-Lira and Roussanov, 2020), let alone the ultimate efficient frontier constructed by individual asset returns. 1 The empirical literature mostly uses ad hoc characteristics-sorted portfolios as test assets (e.g., Fama andFrench, 1993, 1996), which are typically limited to univariate-and bivariate-sorted approaches, due to the difficulties of high-dimensional sorting (Cochrane, 2011). Even with dependent sorting (e.g., Daniel et al., 1997), researchers leave out nonlinearity and asymmetric interactions, instead focus on interactions uniformly applicable to all assets. The inability to capture the efficient frontier hampers the effectiveness of model estimations and evaluations (Lewellen et al., 2010;Ang et al., 2020). The key to bridging the gap between the true efficient frontier and tangency portfolios of assets or factor portfolios lies in systematically utilizing the high-dimensional firm characteristics that contain rich information on the joint distribution of asset returns dynamics. 2 To this end, we introduce the Panel Tree (P-Tree) framework, a new and versatile model family that clusters panel observations to achieve given economic objec-tives. It is adept at analyzing (unbalanced) panel data and inherits the advantages of tree-based models while allowing interpretability under economics-guided global split criteria for goal-oriented search. When applied to the panel of individual asset returns, P-Trees utilize high-dimensional firm characteristics under the MVE framework to jointly generate diversified test assets and latent factors for recovering the stochastic discount factor (SDF). Therefore, they extend the scope of tree models beyond pure prediction tasks, particularly expanding the empirical efficient frontier and constructing diversified basis portfolios, with rich asset pricing and investment implications. 3Specifically, P-Trees employ a top-down approach, splitting the cross section of thousands of individual assets and grouping them into a small number of clusters with similar characteristic values to form value-weighted portfolios. Guided by asset pricing considerations, we grow P-Trees following global split criteria to construct diversified test assets and latent factor models, estimating the efficient frontier. According to Hansen and Jagannathan (1991), the resulting SDF that maximizes the Sharpe ratio by spanning the efficient frontier also minimizes the HJ-distance for explaining the cross section. Generated under the unified framework, the resulting leaf basis portfolios provide empirical researchers with a diversified set of test assets for model evaluation. Furthermore, the decision trees have an intuitive layout, allowing visualized economic interpretability and identifying a sparse set of useful firm characteristics that interact to jointly generate test assets and latent factors.

Fundamentally, P-Tree is a greedy algorithm guided by economic goals for optimal clustering based on firm characteristic values within a large clustering space. In asset pricing, basis portfolios are created by grouping assets based on classifications such as country or industry, or through unsupervised clustering based on the correlation of returns or firm characteristics. By contrast, P-Trees generate characteristicsmanaged leaf basis portfolios to maximize the collective Sharpe ratio of the resulting MVE portfolios, without being either supervised or unsupervised. The objective can be flexibly specified, making the P-Tree framework applicable for a wide range of panel data analyses. 4Methodological innovations. Our emphasis on the asset pricing application effectively demonstrates the key methodological innovations. First, off-the-shelf ML methods, including the famous Classification and Regression Trees (CART, Breiman et al., 1984), typically assume that observations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), and not designed for extracting heterogeneous information from panel data. Though naively fitting CART, boosted trees, or random forests on characteristics-return data shows positive performance (e.g., Gu et al., 2020), they ignore the panel data structure. By contrast, P-Tree fully embraces it and incorporates vectorized leaf parameters tailored for multi-period observations, enabling a time-invariant tree structure for all periods. The time-invariant P-Tree allows for interpretability when building ML models on panel data. As P-Tree grows, its nodes evolve into vectorized values of basis portfolio returns, with the P-Tree factor being their MVE portfolio.

Second, the standard tree-based models in ML, including CART, focus purely on prediction. Furthermore, CART-based models grow recursively, optimizing the quadratic loss of prediction. These models optimize locally at each node without considering sibling nodes, mainly for computational efficiency. However, this "myopic" strategy often leads to overfitting, because it operates on fewer observations in each node as the tree grows. In contrast, P-Trees broaden the applications beyond prediction, encompassing the generation of test assets and latent factors and explaining cross-sectional returns. With an economics-guided optimization objective, the iterative growth of P-Trees is designed to utilize data from the entire cross section to guard against overfitting. P-Tree uses a nonlinear ML approach to generate test assets in asset pricing, maximizing their collective Sharpe ratio with global split criteria. The approach combines economic principles and statistical properties while ensuring transparency and interpretability of individual trees. P-Tree offers the first coherent general approach for creating diversified basis portfolios under the MVE framework. Third, P-Tree seamlessly integrates with ML's boosting strategy, enabling multiple factors to demonstrate exceptional asset pricing and investment performance. As detailed in section 2.3, boosted and multi-factor P-Trees expand the set of assets and factors by exploiting the unspanned efficient frontier under the MVE framework. The multi-factor efficiency of our boosted P-Trees enjoys a natural block-diagonal covariance structure in portfolio construction, achieved by grouping individual assets into P-Tree leaf test assets, without estimating a large covariance matrix of thousands of test assets. Furthermore, P-Trees can assess incremental information on benchmark factor models, such as the Fama-French factors, for interactive and nonlinear modeling of additional characteristics. Overall, when boosted to generate multiple factors, P-Trees offer an alternative to PCA methods, with greater interpretability and sparsity, while capturing (asymmetric) interactions. 5Empirical findings. First, we apply P-Tree to monthly U.S. individual stock returns from 1981 to 2020 using 61 firm characteristics. P-Trees significantly advance the efficient frontier with high annualized Sharpe ratios, ranging from 6.37 for a single P-Tree (with 10 test assets) to 15.63 for 20 boosted P-Trees (with 200 test assets). These numbers are substantially higher than those constructed by conventional basis portfolios (hundreds of univariate-or bivariate-sorted portfolios) or commonly used factor models. These findings provide strong evidence of a significant gap between the current empirical literature and the potential limits of the efficient frontier. Moreover, generated under the unified MVE framework, boosted P-Trees produce multi-factor models that effectively price the cross-sectional returns and offer annualized Sharpe ratios over 3 out-of-sample in the recent 20 years.

Second, these diversified P-Tree test assets span the efficient frontier and pose a significant challenge for alternative factor models. We identify many economically and statistically unexplained test assets, indicated by most monthly alphas larger than 1%, and an extremely high GRS test statistic of 141.27 (aggregated weighted pricing error) for the first P-Tree against the Fama-French five-factor (FF5) model. These asymmetric, interactive, and nonlinear characteristics-managed leaf basis portfolios are difficult to explain using other well-known observable factor models (e.g., Hou et al., 2021) and ML-based latent factor models (e.g., Kelly et al., 2019;Lettau and Pelger, 2020b). Given the insufficient MVE spanning and low hurdles of univariate-or bivariate-sorted portfolios for model testing, we recommend including these multicharacteristic, systematically sorted P-Tree test assets in any future model evaluation. Finally, we design the random P-Forest with bagging to evaluate characteristic importance, account for variable selection risk, and validate transparent and interpretable P-Tree models. We confirm the same small set of characteristics (e.g., SUE, DOLVOL, and BM IA) selected by the P-Tree algorithm is more likely to proxy for the true fundamental risk inherent in the SDF, which may be overlooked in a linear factor model with ad hoc selected factors. In addition, P-Tree offers a novel approach to assess the incremental information of newly added characteristics by controlling for baseline characteristics of size and value, uncovering some characteristics associated with investment, profitability, frictions, and intangibles that contain incremental signals. Last but not least, P-Trees display all split rules, aiding researchers in understanding the interactions among firm characteristics graphically. 6Literature. Foremost, our paper relates to the selection and construction of test assets used for asset pricing model evaluations. The empirical literature, including regularized linear models (e.g., Ao et al., 2019;Kozak et al., 2020;Bryzgalova et al., 2023) and the PCA approaches (e.g., Kozak et al., 2018;Lettau and Pelger, 2020b;Kim et al., 2021), largely takes pre-specified or characteristics-managed portfolios as given. Some evaluate different sets of test assets separately for robustness checks (e.g., Fama andFrench, 1996, 2016), select test assets (e.g., Daniel et al., 2020;Giglio et al., 2022;Bryz-galova et al., 2023), or combine test assets (e.g., Feng et al., 2020;Giglio and Xiu, 2021). Including a large set of test assets presents empirical challenges, such as large portfolio estimation or weak factors (Giglio et al., 2022), leading to the development of new methods for selecting test assets in multiple studies (e.g., Daniel et al., 2020;Zhu et al., 2020). Notably, Bryzgalova, Pelger, and Zhu (2023) shrinks useless assets for estimating the optimal portfolio on a large number of basis portfolios and links security sorting to a collection of decision trees. The authors focus on pruning or regularizing the tree bottom-up without specifying a split criterion for tree growth and manually specify a small set of split candidates and a shallow depth for initial trees (since enumerating all possible tree configurations to prune from is computationally infeasible). P-Trees differ by growing top-down to provide a goal-oriented clustering approach and efficiently scanning the large space of generalized sequential sorting on high-dimensional characteristics, allowing for asymmetric interactions.

Moreover, our study contributes to the growing literature on latent factor models in asset pricing. Early works apply principal component analysis (PCA) to extract latent factors with a purely statistical criterion, such as Chamberlain and Rothschild (1983) and Connor andKorajczyk (1986, 1988). For recent developments, the projected PCA (Kim et al., 2021) and the instrumental PCA (Kelly et al., 2019(Kelly et al., , 2023) ) use firm characteristics as instruments for modeling the time-varying factor loadings and estimating principal components. Lettau and Pelger (2020a,b) develop the risk premia PCA and provide a regularized estimation for risk premia. Recent studies, such as the auto-encoder (Gu et al., 2021), generative adversarial network (Chen et al., 2023), characteristics-sorted factor approximation (Feng et al., 2023), and structural neural network (Fan et al., 2022), have also developed customized deep learning models for nonlinear latent factor modeling. Following these developments, P-Trees provide a graphical representation for variable nonlinearity and asymmetric interactions, which PCA or deep learning methods do not offer. Finally, ML and tree-based methods are widely adopted in finance due to their powerful nonlinear modeling capabilities using high-dimensional characteristics (e.g., Gu et al., 2020;Bianchi et al., 2021;van Binsbergen et al., 2023;Leippold et al., 2022;Bali et al., 2023). However, most studies either apply off-the-shelf ML models for prediction without considering the panel data structure or incorporating economic guidance, or focus on supervised or un-supervised learning. Recent exceptions include Cong et al. (2022), who combine Bayesian spike-and-slab priors and tree models for cross-sectional asset pricing, Cong et al. (2021), who develop the first "large" model in finance for portfolio management using reinforcement learning, and Creal and Kim (2023), who adapt Bayesian trees to currency returns. We also contribute to recent studies advocating imposing economic restrictions when estimating and evaluating ML or factor models (e.g., Gagliardini et al., 2016;Avramov et al., 2023).

Section 2.1 reviews CART and motivates the P-Tree framework. Section 2.2 delves into the growth of P-Trees, before section 2.3 introduces boosted P-Trees for a multi-factor model. The standard CART (Breiman et al., 1984) model and its variants use "divide-andconquer" strategies for making predictions. 7 CART partitions the predictor space into distinct, non-overlapping regions of leaf nodes and assigns a constant leaf parameter to each region (Hastie et al., 2009). It searches and records the partition using a decision tree structure with binary split rules. Suppose the data constitute K predictors, the i-th observation is denoted by z i = (z i,1 , • • • , z i,K ). The j-th split rule of the decision tree is denoted by c(j) = (z •,k , c j ), which partitions data by checking whether the value of the k-th predictor z •,k is greater or smaller than cutoff c j . CART considers only binary splits, since any multiway-split tree can be represented as one with multiple binary splits. The optimal split rule is chosen to minimize the prediction error. After J splits, CART partitions the predictor space into J + 1 leaf nodes denoted by {R n } J+1 n=1 and assigns a constant leaf parameter µ n to each node. The regression tree T , with parameters Θ J = {{c (j) } J j=1 , {µ n } J+1 n=1 }, can be expressed as high-dimensional step functions: The indicator I{z i ∈ R j } takes value 1 for one leaf node and 0 for all others. The leaf parameters, which represent the height of the step function, are estimated by averaging the training data within each leaf node. This nonparametric approach adapts CART to low signal-to-noise environments and small sample sizes. Conventional tree-based models such as CART have multiple limitations, rendering them unsuitable for economic or financial panel data and for generating test assets or pricing kernels. First, they treat asset returns as i.i.d in the cross section or the time series. Second, they focus on predictions using statistical local split criteria, such as minimizing the sum of squared error objectives in the child nodes of a particular split. Therefore, they do not incorporate panel structure or economic restrictions. As the tree grows, the number of observations in each node decreases, and idiosyncratic noise causes overfitting. Although ensemble methods such as random forests reduce overfitting, they are less interpretable than single trees. P-Tree solves both problems by (i) using a vectorized time series of leaf basis portfolio and (ii) using economic objectives that consider all observations instead of just those in a parent node to guide the tree growth. (i) allows us to extract panel data to estimate the efficient frontier thoroughly. Notably, our proposed objective is a global split criterion, because it considers all leaf basis portfolios when constructing F (the global MVE portfolio). Unlike CART, which focuses on a specific leaf node, our model explores all candidate splits in all leaf nodes to find the one with the largest investment improvement.

All subsequent splits are determined in the same manner. The tree-growing procedure is outlined in Algorithm 1. Determining the number of leaves is a natural turning point in tree growth, which is also the only tuning parameter needed for P-Tree. We consider P-Trees with J + 1 = 10 leaf nodes in the baseline specification. Furthermore, we mandate a minimum leaf size of 20 for growing the tree because the leaf needs to serve as a basis portfolio, and any leaves that do not meet this criterion are not subjected to further splitting. Once the tree growing process terminates, it outputs the P-Tree split sequence, leaf basis portfolios R (J) t = [R (J) 1,t , • • • , R (J) J+1,t ], and the P-Tree factor f (J) t . Note each leaf portfolio can be interpreted through economic fundamentals revealed by the sequential splits. Other economically guided criteria The P-Tree framework is flexible to accommodate objectives alternative to the global split criteria in (4) for estimating the MVE portfolio using individual asset returns. For instance, one might seek to create the minimum-variance portfolio or construct latent factors that best explain test assets, such as individual assets or basis portfolio returns. The key lies in specifying a clear economic goal and using the greedy growth algorithm embedded in trees to search the large observation clustering space to optimize the objective effectively.

In Internet Appendix III, we illustrate P-Tree's flexibility using a split criterion based on realized asset pricing errors after estimating a latent factor model with timevarying beta. The asset pricing goal of minimizing pricing errors shares the same spirit in the recent literature for latent factor generation via deep learning (e.g., Gu et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2023;Feng et al., 2023). We run a regression (factor model) for the tree structure and provide a conditional expected value for the leaf parameter. Such P-Trees again produce superior investment and pricing performances.

The panel data has multiple dimensions, so besides splitting the cross section, one can also split the time series, which is an alternative to structural break modeling in econometrics. For future flexible extensions, P-Tree can be extended to consider different macroeconomic regimes and detect those regimes when recursively optimizing the asset pricing objective, fitting regime-specific P-Trees. The data-driven time-series splits of P-Tree are shown by detecting macroinstrumented regimes for cross-sectional asset pricing in Appendix III.D.

Boosting is an ML technique that combines weak learners to form a strong learner (Freund and Schapire, 1997;Rossi and Timmermann, 2015). Boosted P-Trees sequentially grow a list of additive trees that augment previous trees under the MVE framework, which helps further span the efficient frontier with additional basis portfolios and generate multi-factor models. Considering existing factors, the boosting procedure seamlessly integrates into the P-Tree framework by creating additional P-Tree factors to maximize the collective Sharpe ratio of the tangency portfolio. The boosting procedure is outlined below. 1. The initial factor, denoted as f 1,t , can be either generated by the first single P-Tree or benchmark factors selected by researchers (e.g., the market factor). 2. The second factor f 2,t is generated by the second P-Tree to complement the first factor and maximize the squared Sharpe ratio. The second tree growth follows a similar boosting split criterion: where F = [f 1,t , f 2,t ]. The MVE portfolio is generated from all the factors directly. 3. Repeat Step 2 to sequentially generate P factors f t = [f 1,t , • • • , f P,t ] until the stopping criteria are triggered (e.g., one finds insignificant squared Sharpe ratio improvement Barillas and Shanken, 2017). The boosted P-Tree utilizes a two-step process to produce either the MVE portfolio or the SDF by incorporating multiple sets of leaf basis portfolios. Initially, the tree-specific MVE portfolio of all leaf basis portfolios within each P-Tree is computed to determine the current P-Tree factor. Subsequently, this factor is merged with all previous P-Tree factors or benchmarks to create an all-tree MVE portfolio for the multifactor P-Tree model. Boosted P-Trees indirectly impose regularization on the all-tree MVE portfolio weights through the sequential tree block structure, even though the resulting Sharpe ratio may not surpass the one generated directly from all basis portfolios in all P-Trees. This avoids high-dimensional estimation issues and, in turn, leads to robust estimation and out-of-sample performance.

Simulation studies in this section demonstrate the ability of P-Tree models to select characteristics and the effectiveness of P-Tree test assets in capturing non-linear interactions among characteristics. In Appendix I, we calibrate the return-generating process on the same empirical data sample, considering three true characteristics, their interactions, and nonlinear terms. Additionally, we include a large set of redundant characteristics that are correlated with the true characteristics but do not drive returns. First, we compare the Sharpe ratios and alphas of P-Tree test assets with conventional characteristics-sorted portfolios, which cannot model the nonlinear characteristics interactions. The single P-Tree and boosted P-Trees consistently produce leaf basis portfolios with higher Sharpe ratios and larger unexplained pricing errors under various signal-to-noise-ratio levels, both in-sample and out-of-sample. Even though sorting is performed on the true characteristics directly, univariate-and bivariate-sorted portfolios still underperform P-Tree test assets generated on high-dimensional characteristics. This result confirms our empirical findings that P-Tree test assets achieve better mean-variance efficiency than sorted portfolios as in Section 4.2. Second, we demonstrate that P-Tree helps select the sparse true characteristics and a large number of redundant or useless ones. The interpretability of the single P-Tree relies on its ability to select variables. With repeated simulations, we show high frequencies for P-Tree for selecting the true characteristics in the first few splits. These correct selection rates are higher for cases with a high signal-to-noise ratio. This finding can only be identified from simulations, because we remain agnostic regarding the true sparse characteristics in the real-world data. The consistent selection properties are related to evaluating characteristics' importance in Section 5.1.

Finally, we evaluate the efficiency loss without observing all true characteristics but still observe a large set of redundant or useless characteristics. This exercise evaluates the model's performance with incomplete or useless information, which may occur for various reasons. Under our calibrated return-generating process, the Sharpe ratios and CAPM alphas decline substantially, and P-Tree selects redundant or useless characteristics more frequently. Therefore, when a large set of characteristics is provided, we should include all of them rather than performing ad hoc variable selection in empirical studies. For more details, please refer to Appendix I.

First, our simulation evidence in Appendix I demonstrates the efficiency loss resulting from missing true characteristics and illustrates how the nonlinear and interactive P-Tree can recover the true set of characteristics, despite a large number of redundant or useless characteristics. Second, the conventional sequential or independent asset sorting scheme primarily focuses on no more than three characteristics in practice, due to the high-dimensional challenge. Because enumerating all possible sequential sorting cases with multiple characteristics is NP-hard, whether using tree models or not, P-Tree's iterative growth is an efficient algorithm for overcoming this problem and make computation feasible. Therefore, the characteristics selected by the P-Tree algorithm are better proxies for the true fundamental risk inherent in the SDF, which may be overlooked in a linear factor model with ad hoc selected factors. Random P-Forest. We adopt another famous ensembling scheme in ML to evaluate characteristic importance and account for variable selection risk. Random Forest fits multiple trees to avoid overfitting and quantifying model uncertainty. 20 We utilize this approach to assess the significance of variables within the P-Tree framework. In the subsequent text, we refer to our approach as Random P-Forest. The ensemble steps for constructing the Random P-Forest are as follows: (i) bootstrap the data on the time-series horizon with replacement, preserving the complete cross section of the panel data for the selected time periods to exploit the low serial correlations among asset returns. (ii) randomly draw 20 characteristics, and P-Trees grow on each bootstrap sample independently. We repeat the procedure 1,000 times to form a forest of 1,000 P-Trees. (iii) evaluate the importance of each characteristic by counting its appearance in the P-Forest.

Estimating the mean-variance efficient (MVE) frontier and generating diversified test assets using individual asset returns remain long-term challenges in empirical asset pricing (e.g., Markowitz, 1952;Lewellen et al., 2010;Daniel et al., 2020). Our paper presents a novel interpretable AI model, Panel Tree (P-Tree), that effectively addresses the traditional empirical challenge of generalized security sorting and delivers superior performance for analyzing the (unbalanced) panel of individual asset returns. P-Tree utilizes high-dimensional characteristics containing rich information on the joint distribution of asset returns, to generate basis portfolios as diversified test assets and building blocks of the pricing kernel. More generally, P-Trees broaden tree-based models beyond pure prediction and analyze panel data effectively with economics-guided tree growth, while retaining interpretability and handling asymmetric and nonlinear interactions in noisy environments. Our empirical study of U.S. equities shows that the efficient frontiers spanned by P-Tree test assets vastly outperform those from commonly used observable and ma-chine learning latent factor models, as well as conventional test assets. Boosted P-Trees generate sequences of test assets to challenge all existing factor models, providing a diversified test asset alternative to characteristic-sorted portfolios. In addition to leaf basis portfolios, our unified approach under the MVE framework provides tradable P-Tree factors and out-of-sample annualized Sharpe ratios over 3. The factor models also outperform benchmark models in explaining the cross-sectional return variation. Finally, P-Tree offers a new nonlinear and interactive framework to assess the conditional information of high-dimensional characteristics, complementing traditional factor-spanning regression in evaluating firm characteristics.

p.t: Our baseline model generates test assets covering the efficient frontier and constructs the corresponding latent factor, recovering the pricing kernel, maximizing the Sharpe ratio of the MVE portfolio, and minimizing the HJ-distance (Hansen and Jagannathan, 1991). We now demonstrate the flexibility of the P-Tree framework using a criterion that directly minimizes the realized pricing errors of individual stocks. We run a regression model and provide a conditional expected value for the leaf parameter: where r i,t is the excess return for stock i at period t, f t is the P × 1 traded factor return, and β (z i,t-1 ) = b 0 + b z i,t-1 are conditional betas on the past firm characteristics z i,t-1 . The asset pricing goal of minimizing objectives on pricing errors is similar in spirit to the recent literature about latent factor generation for constructing the SDF via deep learning (e.g., Gu et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2023;Feng et al., 2023). With this criterion, P-Tree solves a joint problem of constructing the latent factors and estimating betas. The realized pricing errors are the return residuals from the generated P-Tree factor model. P-Tree generates latent traded factors to reduce the aggregate quadratic realized pricing errors.
